newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS-Steady growth helps Spain's rate prospects.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Steady growth helps Spain's rate prospects.

text.p: The Spanish economy grew 1.9 percent in the second quarter, as expected, leaving the Bank of Spain to focus on politics ahead of an expected quarter-point cut in its key rate next week, economists said on Wednesday.

"The market will focus mainly on the annual rate, the 1.9 percent rise, and that was bang in line with expectations," Gwyn Hacche, senior economist at HSBC James Capel in London, told Reuters Financial Television (RFTV).
Economists polled by Reuters had forecast a rise in gross domestic product (GDP) of 0.8 percent quarter-on-quarter, 1.9 to 2.0 percent year-on-year.
The quarterly figures actually came in somewhat lower at 0.5 percent, but this was partly due to revisions of the first quarter data, Hacche said.

The National Statistics Institute (INE) said first quarter growth had been revised to a rise of 0.6 percent quarter-on-quarter, 2.0 percent year-on-year, compared with the previous figures of 0.8 percent and 1.9 percent respectively.

Spanish analysts said the figures mean the government is likely to achieve its 1996 growth target of 2.3 percent, a forecast it relies on to reduce the 1997 budget deficit to the level required to join a single European currency.
The data also leave the Bank of Spain free to focus on the 1997 budget due to be presented on Monday and which is expected to be followed by a rate cut the day after.

"(Recovery) in the third and fourth quarters will help us reach a growth rate of 2.3 or 2.25 percent for 1996 and a number around 2.5 percent in 1997," Alfredo Urrutia, capital markets economist at Societe Generale in Madrid, told RFTV.
"The scenario for rates remains the same," said Carmen Hernansaez, economist at FG in Madrid. "The Bank of Spain is more focused on politics and the upcoming budget."
Some analysts doubted, however, that Spain could meet its growth and budget deficit targets.
"I personally doubt that the government can reach 2.3 percent this year and I think there is a risk that for next year, the figure may fall below 2.5 percent," said Hacche.

He forecast Spain's budget deficit would fall below four percent of GDP next year but fail to satisfy the Maastricht target of a 3.0 percent ratio needed to join the first wave of monetary union (EMU) in 1999. He thought the government might also miss its inflation target of 2.6 percent in 1997.
Others, like Alfredo Urrutia, said Spain could narrowly miss the three percent budget deficit target in 1997 but would join a single currency in a second membership phase.
"I think Spain will come pretty close to the mark (on next year's budget deficit target). It has a chance to make it not on Day One, but on Day Two", he said.

Analysts said the recovery in private consumption remained the main motor for growth in the second half of the year. Consumption rose 1.9 percent compared with a revised 1.7 percent in the first quarter.

"I would single out two factors," said Hernansaez. "The recovery of private consumption, which continues to be the key to Spain achieving its annual growth target, and the rise in exports with a strong revision of first quarter figures."
The INE said exports rose 9.1 percent in the second quarter and revised the first quarter figure up to 8.7 percent from 5.3 percent previously.
